prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms opened the 10^-18 regime of time measurement

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye, and the first-round exchange has sharpened rather than weakened my reasons. The chair asks whether the lattice clock is a distinct invention after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is, and the distinction is physical, not a matter of degree. The comb made optical cycles countable and ion control showed that a single well-isolated particle can serve as a clock. The lattice clock solved a different problem: how to keep the freedom from Doppler and recoil shifts of a trapped particle while interrogating of order a million atoms, which is only possible because at the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel. That is a new physical idea, proposed by Katori, demonstrated in strontium, and then driven to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 by Ye's group with many-body clock physics and cavity-stabilised lasers. The result has been reproduced and intercompared over fibre by independent laboratories in several countries, and it has made millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for drifting constants and relativistic geodesy experimentally real. As a theorist who sits close to experimental teams, this is the kind of result I trust: a quantum system controlled in every physical detail, with agreement across laboratories. I would anchor the citation on the invention and the many-atom realization, not on the record number, which will keep moving. I do not require the redefinition of the second for the prize; the discovery is the physics, not its metrological adoption.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains adjacency: a third prize in precision spectroscopy and atomic clocks within about twenty years, and an achievement that improves how well we measure time rather than revealing a new phenomenon of nature, a standard Lindroth and Danielsson apply with some force. I have not fully dissolved that objection; I have argued that the lattice concept is a distinct idea, and a reasonable colleague may still judge it an excellent continuation. The attribution to two names is a judgement, because Lemonde, Takamoto, Boyd and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups made early and important contributions, and Ye's records rest on comb, laser-stabilisation and large-team work. The formal redefinition of the second is still pending, so some will see the timing as early. Finally, I note an asymmetry in my own reasoning: I used 2025 proximity to move away from circuit QED, and I must apply the same standard of adjacency to B035 and B008 and not only to the candidate close to my own field.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the lattice clock is chiefly a gain in precision whereas IceCube found something nature had not told us before, and he would resist trimming Karle from the IceCube trio. He also says he would not oppose a clock prize if the IceCube credit proves too diffuse.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between surprise and precision as a real criterion, and IceCube clearly passes it. My answer is that precision here is not just more digits: tests of gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings are measurements of nature that were out of reach before, and the lattice concept is what made them possible. On IceCube I still defer to you and Pearce on weight, but you concede yourself that the allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and the AMANDA and DUMAND founders cannot be made airtight, and I find the lattice-clock credit easier to defend. I have moved IceCube from outside my alternatives to second alternative, because your argument that the diffuse flux is secure independent of source identifications is persuasive to me, and I would not oppose it if an expert report settled the credit.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the 2016 prize covered the integer quantum Hall and Thouless-Haldane lineage and BKT transitions, whereas the Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall state are a distinct discovery, and that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap is real but can be handled by wording the citation around the prediction of the state and its first observation.
responses.response: This is a fair correction to my round-1 reading. I raised 2016 as a possible overlap, and your distinction between the Thouless-Haldane lineage and time-reversal-invariant Z2 topology is convincing, so I no longer count 2016 as a strong objection to B008 and I would apply one standard of adjacency to both B008 and B035: both are separate discoveries that sit near an earlier prize. My remaining difficulty is credit. A citation on the Kane-Mele prediction and the HgTe realization is defensible, but BHZ made the specific proposal for HgTe that told Molenkamp what to measure, and the 3D generalization lies outside the trio, so I cannot call that configuration settled. I would support B008 as the committee's choice if the colleagues in condensed matter find that wording adequate, and I keep it as my first alternative, but I do not move it above B035 because the attribution problem is larger and I cannot judge it from first-hand knowledge.

responses.point: Kroll supports B035 and argues that the lattice clock differs from single-ion clocks because it reaches comparable accuracy while interrogating about a million atoms, giving stability that single ions cannot match; he also discloses a loose link to the Hall and JILA environment.
responses.response: I agree and would build the citation on exactly that point: the lattice concept delivers both the freedom from motional shifts of a trapped particle and the signal-to-noise of many atoms. That is the sharpest answer to the chair's first question. I would resist wording that implies a mere extension of the ion clock, and I would also leave out a specific accuracy figure. On attribution I accept your view that SYRTE and PTB mostly confirmed and refined after the Katori proposal and the first Ye accuracy demonstrations, but I do not think that can be asserted from our own memory, so I support asking for an external priority check on the early strontium and ytterbium results before the final vote. Your disclosure of the Hall link seems to me minor and not a reason for recusal, and I note that it does not extend to Katori.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B035 and stresses that the lattice clock is trustworthy because the magic wavelength and blackbody shift depend on atomic-structure theory checked repeatedly against experiment, while conceding that a topological or tunable-matter discovery may reveal more about nature than a better clock.
responses.response: Your point about agreement between atomic-structure calculation and experiment is, for me, the strongest robustness argument, because the systematic corrections can be cross-checked by theory and by independent clocks. I also agree that you apply the surprise standard honestly. Where I would push back mildly is the idea that a clock must be judged chiefly as a measurement instrument: the lattice clock also made new physics accessible, including many-body spin-exchange and collective effects in the lattice, which Ye's group studied directly. I respect that you place B008 above B035 on conceptual depth. Our difference is mainly attribution, where your own round-1 view that the clock has no BHZ-type allocation problem seems to me the deciding practical consideration.

uncertainties: Whether a lattice-clock prize is accepted by the committee as a distinct achievement after the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I have argued it is but the judgement remains open.
Whether an external expert report on early strontium and ytterbium lattice-clock priority would change the fair credit beyond Katori and Ye, in particular for Lemonde, Takamoto and Boyd.

Whether the committee would apply the same adjacency standard to B008 and the 2016 prize as to B035, and whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap can be resolved in the citation wording; I cannot judge the condensed-matter details first-hand.
For IceCube I rely on colleagues in astroparticle physics for how to credit work in a collaboration of hundreds.
Whether my reluctance on circuit QED is a fair application of the gap-after-2025 principle or an over-correction caused by closeness to that community; a later year might change this.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My possible recusal issue is for B004 (circuit QED) and B012 (squeezing), through my work in superconducting circuits at Chalmers, my directorship of WACQT, which has hosted Martinis and Clarke as guest researchers, and long ties to Per Delsing's group and the circuit-QED community. I have therefore not led the argument for either, and I would step back from the vote if B004 became the leading candidate. In response to the chair's question, I see no need for any member to step back from the discussion of B035, B008 or B023. I have no known connection to Katori, Ye, the lattice-clock community, the topological-insulator authors or IceCube. Kroll's disclosed WACQT leadership overlaps institutionally with my own, but it does not bear on B035.
